¶
'''buffet<sup>1</sup>''' (buf′et), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''buffeted'', ppr. ''buffeting''. [< ME. ''buffeten'', ''bofeten'' = Icel. ''buffeita'' (cf. Sp. ''bofetear'', ''abofetear'', Pg. ''bofetear'' = It. ''buffetare'', ''boffettegiare''—Florio), buffet; from the noun.] '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To strike with the hand or fist; box; beat.
{{smaller block|Then did they spit in his face, and ''buffeted'' him; and others smote him with the palms of their hands.
{{right|Mat. xxvi. 67.}}}}
'''2.''' To beat in contention; contend against as if with blows: as, to ''buffet'' the billows.
{{smaller block|<poem>The torrent roar’d; and we did ''buffet'' it
With lusty sinews; throwing it aside
And stemming it with hearts of controversy.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', J. C., i. 2.}}}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To exercise at boxing; box; contend with blows of the fists; hence, to force one’s way by buffeting.
{{smaller block|If I might ''buffet'' for my love, . . . I could lay on like a butcher.
{{right|''Shak.'', Hen. V., v. 2.}}
<poem>I caught her; then
Oaring one arm, and bearing in my left
The weight of all the hopes of half the world,
Strove to ''buffet'' to land in vain.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Princess, iv.}}}}

'''buffet<sup>2</sup>''' (buf′et, or, as F., bü-fā′), ''n.'' [Sometimes
readings.c1s3:
erroneously written ''beaufet'' (simulating F. ''beau'', fine—a notion present, in another form, in the orig. use), < ME. ''buffitt, buffit, boffet, bofet'' (in def. 4, and comp. ''buffet-stool'', q. v.) = D. G. Dan. Sw. ''buffet'' = Russ. ''bufetŭ'', a sideboard, = Sp. Pg. ''bufete'', a desk, writing-table, Pg. also a sideboard, < F. ''buffet'', a sideboard, a cupboard, in older F. esp. of an elegant or costly kind, “a court cupboord, or high-standing cupboord, also a cupboord of plate, also as much plate as will furnish a cupboord” (Cotgrave), also a desk or writing-table, < It. ''buffetto'', formerly also ''boffetto'', a cupboard, sideboard, buffet (ML. ''bufetum'', a buffet, cf. ''buffetus'', a council; cf. ''bureau'' in similar senses), appar. so called from its elegance, being = OF. ''bufoi, buffois'', sumptuousness, show, pomp, fine equipage, < ''bufer, buffer'' (= It. ''buffare'', etc.), puff, blow: see ''buff''<sup>2</sup>, and cf. ''buffet''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1.''' A cupboard, sideboard, or closet, designed to hold china, crystal, plate, and other like articles.—'''2.''' The space set apart for refreshments in public places.—'''3.''' That part of the cabinet-work of an organ which incloses the pipes.—'''4.''' Same as ''buffet-stool''. ''Wright'', Prov. Dict. [Prov. Eng.]

'''buffeter''' (buf′et-ėr), ''n.'' One who buffets or strikes with the hand or fist; a boxer.

'''buffeting''' (buf′et-ing), ''n.'' [Verbal n. of ''buffet''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.''] A beating; a blow; a buffet.
{{smaller block|He had withstood these ''buffetings'' to the last till sickness overtook him.
{{right|''Sterne'', Tristram Shandy, vi. 13.}}}}

'''buffet-stool''' (buf′et-stöl), ''n.'' [< ME. ''buffett''

'''buffing''' (buf′ing), ''n.'' [< ''buff''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ing''<sup>1</sup>.] The operation of diminishing the thickness of a hide by means of a curriers’ knife or a splitting-machine, for the purpose of increasing the suppleness of the leather; hence, the layer so shaved off; the amount of lessening effected.
{{smaller block|When about one-third tanned, the hides are removed from the tanning liquor and a ''buffing'' is taken off of each hide.
{{right|''C. T. Davis'', Leather, p. 586.}}}}

'''buffing-lathe''' (buf′ing-lāᴛ̵ʜ), ''n.'' A lathe in which metal plates are polished. The buffer may be of leather, cotton, or other material, and is used with various polishing-powders.

'''buffing-machine''' (buf′ing-ma-shēn″), ''n.'' A machine used for buffing or polishing.

'''buffing-spring''' (buf′ing-spring), ''n.'' Same as ''buffer-spring.''

'''buffing-wheel''' (buf′ing-hwēl), ''n.'' Same as ''buff-wheel.''

'''buff-jerkin''' (buf′jėr″kin), ''n.'' '''1.''' A garment formerly worn under the corselet, and made of buff-leather, whence its name. It took the place of the acton and gambeson.—'''2.''' A waistcoat made of buff-leather; hence, a waistcoat made of cloth of a buff color. {{smaller|It seems to have been con-}}

'''buffoonery''' (bu-fön′ėr-i), ''n.''; pl. ''buffooneries'' (-iz). [< ''buffoon'' + ''-ery'', after F. ''bouffonnerie.''] The art and practices of a buffoon; low jests; ridiculous pranks; vulgar tricks and postures.

'''buffoonize†''' (bu-fön′īz), ''v. t.'' [< ''buffoon'' + ''-ize.''] To jest. ''Minsheu'', 1617.

'''buffoonly''' (bu-fön′li), ''a.'' [< ''buffoon'' + ''-ly''<sup>1</sup>.] Buffoonish. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Apish tricks and ''buffoonly'' discourse.

'''buffo-singer''' (bü′ō-sing″ėr), ''n.'' A singer of comic songs in opera bouffe; a buffo.

'''buff-stick''' (buf′stik), ''n.'' A piece of stick covered with leather, velvet, velveteen, or other material, and charged with emery or other powder, used in polishing.

'''buff-tip''' (buf′tip), ''n.'' '''1.''' A name of a Japanese shrike, ''Lanius bucephalus'', so called because of a buff patch on the wing.—'''2.''' A name of a moth similarly marked.

'''buffum''' (buf′um), ''n.'' [Origin obscure.] A mixture of several inferior kinds of oil, used as an adulterant of linseed-oil. ''Encyc. Brit.'' [Eng.]

'''buff-ware''' (buf′wãr), ''n.'' In ''ceram.'', a stoneware made in Staffordshire, England, from the clay and other ingredients found there, and not decorated. {{smaller|The name is derived from the natural color}}

'''buffet'''<sup>1</sup> (buf′et), ''n.''   [< ME. ''buffet, boffet, bofet'' (= Icel. ''buffeit''), < OF. ''buffet, bufet'' (= It. ''buffeto'', formerly ''buffetto, boffetto''; cf. Sp. Pg. ''bofetada''), a blow, < ''buffe, bufe'', a blow: see ''buff''<sup>2</sup>.]   '''1.''' A blow with the fist; a box; a cuff; a slap; hence, hard usage of any kind suggestive of blows; a violent shock or concussion: as, “fortune’s ''buffets'',” ''Shak.'', Hamlet, iii. 2.
{{smaller block|The kynge redressed hym and yaf hym soche a ''buffet'' vpon the lefte temple that the blode braste oute of mouthe and nose.
{{right|''Merlin'' (E. E. T. S.), iii. 391.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>For God’s sake, sir, be merry, or else bear
The ''buffets'' of your fortune with more scorn!</poem>
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Honest Man’s Fortune, iv. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|We get . . . many a ''buffet'' of the rough water of experience, before we secure the bare right to live.
{{right|''Lowell'', Fireside Travels, p. 138.}}}}
'''2†.''' A blast of wind.
{{smaller block|Thay blwe a ''buffet'' in blande that banned peple.
{{right|''Alliterative Poems'' (ed. Morris), ii. 885.}}}}

{{right|''Tennyson'', Princess, iv.}}}}

'''buffle†''', ''n.'' Same as ''buff''<sup>4</sup>.   ''Florio.''

{{smaller block|When about one-third tanned, the hides are removed from the tanning liquor and a ''buffing'' is taken off of each hide.
{{right|''C. T. Davis'', Leather, p. 586.}}}}

'''buffing-block''' (buf′ing-blok), ''n.'' Same as ''buffer-block.''

'''buffing-lathe''' (buf′ing-lāᴛ̵ʜ), ''n.'' A lathe in which metal plates are polished. The buffer may be of leather, cotton, or other material, and is used with various polishing-powders.

'''buffing-machine''' (buf′ing-ma-shēn″), ''n.'' A machine used for buffing or polishing.

'''buffing-spring''' (buf′ing-spring), ''n.'' Same as ''buffer-spring.''

'''buffing-wheel''' (buf′ing-hwēl), ''n.'' Same as ''buff-wheel.''

'''buff-jerkin''' (buf′jėr″kin), ''n.'' '''1.''' A garment formerly worn under the corselet, and made of buff-leather, whence its name. It took the place of the acton and gambeson.—'''2.''' A waistcoat made of buff-leather; hence, a waistcoat made of cloth of a buff color. {{smaller|It seems to have been considered}} the peculiar mark of constables and other officers of the law.

{{smaller block|<poem>Fighting! what’s fighting? it may be in fashion
Among provant swords, and ''buff-jerkin'' men.</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher (and another)'', Elder Brother, v. 1.}}}}

'''buff-laced''' (buf′lāst), ''a.'' In ''poultry-'' and ''pigeon-breeding'', having the feathers laced or edged with buff: said of birds of which the color is a rich buff, each feather being distinctly laced with pale buff, as in the case of ''buff-laced'' Polish fowls, or of birds of which the color is pale buff, each feather being laced with dark buff.

'''buffle'''<sup>1</sup> (buf′l), ''n.''   [< F. ''buffle'', a buffalo.]   '''1.''' A buffalo.—'''2.''' A duck, ''Bucephala albeola'', abundant in North America. {{smaller|It has a short blue bill and}} a head the apparent size of which is greatly increased by
{{smaller|the fullness of its feathers. The male is chiefly black above and white below, the head being iridescent-black with a large white occipital space. Also called ''buffle-head'', ''buffle-duck'', ''buffle-headed duck'', ''spirit-duck'', ''dipper'', and ''butterball''. Also spelled ''buffel''.}}

'''buff-leather''' (buf′le″ᴛ̵ʜėr), ''n.'' Same as ''buff''<sup>1</sup>, 2.

'''buffle-duck''' (buf′l-duk), ''n.'' Same as ''buffle''<sup>1</sup>, 2.

'''buffle-head''' (buf′l-hed), ''n.'' '''1†.''' One who has a large or stupid head, like a buffalo’s. {{smaller block|What makes you stare so, ''buffle-head?''
{{right|''Plautus'' (trans.), 1694.}}}}
'''2.''' Same as ''buffle''<sup>1</sup>, 2.

'''buffle-headed†''' (buf′l-hed″ed), ''a.'' Having a large head, like a buffalo’s; dull; stupid; foolish.   ''Gayton'', Notes on Don Quixote, III. 3.

'''buffle-horn''' (buf′l-hôrn), ''n.'' The common name in South Africa of the ''Burchellia Capensis'', on account of the hardness and toughness of the wood. {{smaller|It is a rubiaceous shrub, with handsome flowers, sometimes cultivated in hothouses.}}

'''buffle-wood''' (buf′l-wu̇d), ''n.'' Same as ''buffle-horn.''

'''buffo''' (buf′ō), ''n.''   [It., a comic actor, also a puff, whiff, < ''buffare'', puff, rally, mock: see ''buff''<sup>2</sup>, ''buffoon.'']   The comic actor in an opera; a comic singer.

'''buffon,''' ''n.'' Same as ''buffont.''

'''buffont†,''' ''n.''   [< F. ''bouffant'' (cf. “''bouffancs'' [sic], puffs in a garment”—Cotgrave), ppr. of ''bouffer,'' puff out: see ''buff''<sup>2</sup>, ''buffet''<sup>1</sup>.]   A projecting or puffed-out covering of gauze or linen for the breast, much worn by women about the middle of the eighteenth century.

'''buffoon''' (bu-fön′), ''n.'' and ''a.''   [< F. ''bouffon,'' < It. ''buffone'' (= Sp. ''bufon'' = Pg. ''bufão''), a jester, < ''buffa'' (= Sp. ''bufa''), a jest, mocking, connected with ''buffare'' (= Pr. Sp. Pg. ''bufar'' = F. ''bouffer''), puff, blow: see ''buff''<sup>2</sup>, ''buffet''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''I.''' ''n.'' One who makes a practice of amusing others by tricks, odd gestures and postures, jokes, and other vulgar pleasantries; a droll; a merry-andrew; a clown; a jester.
{{smaller block|The scurril talk of ''buffoons,'' pleasants, and jesters.
{{right|''Holland,'' tr. of Plutarch, p. 487.}}}}
{{smaller block|''Buffoons'' that have a talent of mimicking the speech and behaviour of other persons. {{right|''Tatler,'' No. 268.}}}}
{{smaller|='''Syn.''' See ''zany.''}}

'''II.''' ''a.'' Characteristic of a buffoon; buffoonish.
{{smaller block|Neither ''buffoon'' nor contemptible. {{right|''Lamb,'' Old Actors.}}}}
{{smaller block|''Buffoon'' stories. {{right|''Macaulay,'' Hist. Eng., xiv.}}}}

'''buffoon''' (bu-fön′), ''v.''   [< ''buffoon,'' ''n.'']   '''I.''' ''intrans.'' To act the part of a buffoon.   ''Dryden.'' [Rare.]

'''II.''' ''trans.'' To make ridiculous. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Religion . . . despised, ''buffooned,'' exposed as ridiculous.
{{right|''Glanville,'' Sermons, ix. 343.}}}}
{{smaller block|Went to see the Duke of Buckingham’s ridiculous farce and rhapsody, called “The Recital,” ''buffooning'' all plays, yet prophane enough. {{right|''Evelyn,'' Diary, Dec. 14, 1671.}}}}

'''buffoonery''' (bu-fön′ėr-i), ''n.''; pl. ''buffooneries'' (-iz).   [< ''buffoon'' + ''-ery'', after F. ''bouffonnerie.'']   The art and practices of a buffoon; low jests; ridiculous pranks; vulgar tricks and postures.
{{smaller block|<poem>No merit was secure, no person free
From its licentious ''buffoonery.''</poem>
{{right|''Oldham'', Horace’s Art of Poetry.}}}}

'''buffoonish''' (bu-fön′ish), ''a.''   [< ''buffoon'' + ''-ish''<sup>1</sup>.]   Like a buffoon; consisting in buffoonery.   ''Blair.''

'''buffoonism''' (bu-fön′izm), ''n.''   [< ''buffoon'' + ''-ism.'']   The practices of a buffoon; buffoonery.

'''buffoonize†''' (bu-fön′īz), ''v. t.''   [< ''buffoon'' + ''-ize.'']   To jest.   ''Minsheu'', 1617.

'''buffoonly''' (bu-fön′li), ''a.''   [< ''buffoon'' + ''-ly''<sup>1</sup>.]   Buffoonish. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Apish tricks and ''buffoonly'' discourse.
{{right|''J. Goodman'', Winter Eve. Conference, 1.}}}}

'''buffo-singer''' (bü′ō-sing″ėr), ''n.'' A singer of comic songs in opera bouffe; a buffo.

'''buff-stick''' (buf′stik), ''n.'' A piece of stick covered with leather, velvet, velveteen, or other material, and charged with emery or other powder, used in polishing.

'''buff-tip''' (buf′tip), ''n.'' '''1.''' A name of a Japanese shrike, ''Lanius bucephalus'', so called because of a buff patch on the wing.—'''2.''' A name of a moth similarly marked.

'''buffum''' (buf′um), ''n.''   [Origin obscure.]   A mixture of several inferior kinds of oil, used as an adulterant of linseed-oil.   ''Encyc. Brit.'' [Eng.]

'''buff-ware''' (buf′wãr), ''n.'' In ''ceram.'', a stoneware made in Staffordshire, England, from the clay and other ingredients found there, and not decorated. {{smaller|The name is derived from the natural color of the clay when fired.}}

'''buff-wheel''' (buf′hwēl), ''n.'' A wheel of wood, glue, leather, light fabrics, or other material, used with emery, rouge, or other powders in polishing glass and metals. Also called ''buffer'' and ''buffing-wheel.''

'''buffy''' (buf′i), ''a.''   [< ''buff''<sup>1</sup> + ''-y''<sup>1</sup>.]   Buff-colored; pertaining to buff on the blood.—{{smaller|'''Buffy coat''', the coat of fibrin free from red blood-corpuscles on the upper surface of a blood-clot, which is formed when the coagulation is delayed until after the corpuscles have sunk so as to leave the upper layers of the blood.}}

'''Bufo''' (bū′fō), ''n.''   [L., a toad.]   A genus of tailless amphibians, typical of the family ''Bufonidæ'', and embracing the common toads of Europe and North America. See cut under ''agua-toad.''

'''bufonid''' (bū′fọ̄-nid), ''n.'' An amphibian of the family ''Bufonidæ.''

'''Bufonidæ''' (bụ̄-fon′i-dē), ''n. pl.''   [NL., < ''Bufo(n-)'' + ''-idæ.'']   A family of arciferous salient amphibians, typified by the genus ''Bufo'', without maxillary teeth and with dilated sacral vertebræ and a broad flat tongue, free behind; the toads. {{smaller|The body and limbs are thick, heavy, and clumsy, and the skin is warty or rugose. The species are less aquatic than frogs, not arboreal like tree-toads, and much less agile. About 100 species are known. See cut under ''agua-toad.''}}

'''bufoniform''' (bụ̄-fon′i-fôrm), ''a.''   [< L. ''bufo(n-)'', a toad, + ''forma'', shape.]   Having the form of a toad; resembling a toad; bufonoid; specifically, of or pertaining to the ''Bufoniformia'': contrasted with ''raniform.''<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
